sources.title: M.H. Kalavathy, Ethnical and Socio-Cultural Background of Marine Fishing Communities in Orissa, in U. Tietze (ed.), Artisanal Marine Fisherfolk of Orissa
sources.publication: Vidyapuri, Cuttack, first published December1985; BOBP/MIS/3, FAO-hosted scan
sources.status: actual original chapter, title/imprint and introduction inspected
sources.locator: Chapter3 section3.1.2, printed62–63 (chapterPDF4–5); introduction printed5–6; frontmatterPDF4 imprint
claims: In its northern Odisha discussion the1985 study explicitly connects Kaibarta with Kewat or Keota. Preserve source-specific scope rather than imposing a universal alias rule.

It distinguishes Chasi and Jalia/Adi Kaibarta: cultivation and river/estuary fishing were associated with different histories, but livelihoods overlapped and both could engage in sea-fishing. This contradicts a timeless single-occupation account.
The author does not know exactly when the move to sea-fishing occurred. Her approximate sixty-years-earlier suggestion is an assumption, not a foundation date; omit numerical extrapolation.
The study compared248households in ten selected villages: six in then-Balasore and four in Ganjam. Interviews and observations included men and women; authors acknowledge limited observation time.
limits: No exact fieldwork dates verified; use study published1985, never survey2004.
2004 is FAO website copyright, not original publication.
Chapter draws partly on older ethnography and should be described as a period study, not present-day demographic truth.
Do not import caste-rank or enterprising-character praise, surname lists as identity tests, or universal gender-role prescriptions.
Do not transfer southern Telugu communities' festivals in section3.3 to Kaibarta.
sources.rights: FAO landing page permits attributed educational/noncommercial reproduction, requires permission for resale/commercial uses. Do not assume an unrestricted image license. Frontmatter credits photos to E.Amalore, M.H.Kalavathy and U.Tietze.

sources.title: Vasudha Chhotray, Justice at Sea: Fishers’ politics and marine conservation in coastal Odisha, India
sources.locator: Introduction methodology paragraphs; section Social relations amongst fishers and the construction of Odiya environmentalism
claims: Original research comprised approximately ten group discussions and forty long interviews, November2011–May2012, around three Kendrapara village cases. It is purposive local research, not an Odisha-wide survey.
The study describes Kaibarta organisation through Kalinga Karnadhar Fishermen’s Society, founded1962. Its leader's1861royal-grant story is reported testimony, not a verified charter.

Different interviewees gave opposing accounts of a fishing-rights court dispute; the researcher explicitly did not independently establish its outcome. This is useful evidence of contested memory, not proof of exclusive contemporary rights.

Her fieldwork describes weakened central association authority, livelihood pressures and changes towards motorised gill-net fishing among some Odia fishers. Ethnic contrasts promoted by leaders did not fully describe everyday cooperation or shared economic pressures.
limits: Village names are pseudonyms according to footnote1; do not add them to geographic tourism maps or infer actual locations.
Do not generalise allegations or vigilance incidents to an entire caste.
Do not present legal rights, citizenship allegations or conservation rules as current verified law.
Erratum checked: editorial/reference corrections, not a replacement for the Kaibarta passages.
sources.rights: Article is open access. No image selected; maps locate broader research landscape and do not depict community identity.

sources.title: Basista Kumar Behera, Chaiti Ghoda: At the Door of Extinction
sources.status: actual two-page original inspected; parent also independently inspected
sources.locator: Printed10 final paragraph and printed11; filename11–12 does not match printedpages
claims: Behera describes Ghoda Nata as a Kaibarta festival beginning at Chaitra full moon, with village-road songs and performances, contributions of money and cloth, and gatherings of performing parties.

He recounts multiple origin traditions, including Rama's gift of a horse after a fisherman assisted a river crossing and a Dasraj rescue narrative associated with Kaibarta Geeta. Present these as stories recounted by Behera, not historical caste formation.
The Kaibarta Geeta itself was not inspected.
limits: Do not repeat speculative hero-worship explanation as established origin.
Do not reproduce obsolete/incorrect district attribution for Chudamani.
No basis to claim this form of festival is universal or unchanged today; source2012.
No contemporary extinction status established by article title.

narrative_plan: Central question: how did a community associated with rivers and estuaries change with new fishing grounds, technologies and institutions?
Introduce1985 northern-coast evidence, name relationship with precise scope, and cultivation/fishing overlap.
Explain that a documented occupation or later transition does not tell us when a caste was created; no single-founder claim is justified.
Use Chaiti Ghoda as a specific community practice carrying remembered origin stories. Choose one story and retain attribution rather than squeezing every legend into the article.
Use2011–12 fieldwork to show institutions and livelihoods changing, with disputed history honestly qualified. Avoid amplifying hostile ethnic allegations or treating heritage as exclusive rights.
Close with open questions about local family histories, training, river knowledge and current practice; no invented survey or modern ritual uniformity.
